newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil re-election bill reaches Senate.
newsitem.headline: Brazil re-election bill reaches Senate.

text.p: An amendment of Brazil's constitution, which would allow President Fernando Henrique Cardoso to run for re-election next year, was presented to the Senate Wednesday, a day after after it cleared the lower house.
Chamber of Deputies president Deputy Michel Temer handed a copy of the draft legislation to his upper house counterpart Senator Antonio Carlos Magalhaes, a congressional official said.
Magalhaes said he expected the bill would be put to a first vote on the floor of the Senate in March and a second and final vote in April, local newswire Invest News reported.
The bill should be "voted on with the kind of speed expected by public opinion and with the same urgency as in the lower house," the newswire quoted Magalhaes as saying.
State governors and mayors would also be allowed to run for a second consecutive term if the reform is approved.

The amendment won 368 votes in the Chamber of Deputies late Tuesday in its second and final vote there, 60 more than the three-fifths majority needed and 32 more than when it was first approved in January.
An addendum to the bill approved Tuesday specifies that executive office-holders may only run for one additional term.

The bill is now due to be studied in the Senate's Constitution and Justice Committee before being put to its two votes on the floor of the upper house, each requiring a three-fifths majority for approval.

Observers say the re-election bill is likely to face a smoother ride in the normally sedate Senate than in the Chamber of Deputies, where a threatened boycott of the bill by so-called government allies in January put its first approval at risk.
Some pitfalls may lie along the government's way, however.
A group of senators are believed to favor altering the amendment to force sitting governors and mayors to stand down during their re-election campaigns.
Such a change would help the senators' own electoral ambitions, but would would require another round of voting in the lower house, which the government wants to avoid.
Another potential problem for re-election in the upper house is the government's controversial pension reform bill, which is currently being rewritten by a government-allied senator.
That bill is expected to reach the Senate floor within two months and could prove a distraction if re-election has not been approved by then.

There may also be damaging fallout from an ongoing inquiry by a Senate panel, police and the government's financial watchdog, the Federal Accounts Tribunal, into an alleged, multi-million dollar fraud involving state and municipal debt.
